The title key sets each object's display name; keep a stable id as the primary key.
Q012727:
## Base types set what a property can do
A property's base type defines what data it holds and which operations applications offer for it. Besides common types (String, Integer, Date ...), the base types page lists advanced types:
- **Geopoint**: geographic points, stored as `latitude,longitude` (for example `57.64911,10.40744`).
- **Geoshape**: geographic shapes such as areas.
- **Vector**: vectors for semantic search.
- **Struct**: schema-based properties with several fields.

Example: depot `D-17` gets `52.37,4.90` as its location property.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Geopoint (correct):** the base type the docs define for geographic points, holding latitude and longitude together in one value that map features can use.
- ✗ **B. Vector:** the docs describe vectors for semantic search, not map locations.
- ✗ **C. Struct:** a generic multi-field type; it does not give the property geographic meaning.
- ✗ **D. Geoshape:** meant for shapes; a depot location is a single point.

Q012728:
## How link types are stored
The create link type guide offers three ways to back a link type:
- **Foreign keys**: one-to-one or one-to-many. A property on one object type stores the primary key of the other, like a foreign key column in a relational database.
- **Join table dataset**: many-to-many. A dataset lists the pairs of primary keys.
- **Backing object type**: an intermediary object type carries the link plus extra metadata.
## Matching the shape of the data
Here the carrier code already sits on each shipment and each shipment has exactly one carrier. That is the textbook foreign key case: Foundry creates a link wherever a shipment's carrier code equals a carrier's primary key.
Example: shipment `SH-9921` has carrier code `DHL-NL`; the link joins it to the `Carrier` object with that primary key, and from the carrier you can traverse to all its shipments.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Copy carrier properties:** duplicates data and gives up navigation from a carrier to its shipments.
- ✓ **B. Foreign key, one-to-many (correct):** the shipment property that holds the carrier's primary key backs the link directly.
- ✗ **C. Object-backed link:** an intermediary object is for links that need their own properties, not for every one-to-many case.
- ✗ **D. Join table for every link:** join tables are for many-to-many relationships; foreign key links need no extra dataset.

## Key idea
A property that holds another type's primary key backs a one-to-many link type by foreign key.
Q012729:
## Many-to-many needs a join table
A foreign key can only hold one value per object, so it suits one-to-one and one-to-many relationships. For many-to-many relationships the create link type guide uses a join table dataset whose columns match the primary keys of both object types. The guide adds that a many-to-many link with a backing datasource is required to let users edit or write back to the link type, and it can generate an empty join table with the right schema for you.
## One link type, two directions
A link type is bidirectional: it has two sides and can be traversed from either object type, so there is no need for a second "reverse" link type.
Example: the join table holds rows such as `T-042, CERT-HV` and `T-042, CERT-GAS`; an action that adds a certification creates a new link row.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. One-to-one:** the docs state one-to-one cardinality is an indicator and is not enforced, and the real relationship is many-to-many anyway.
- ✗ **B. Two link types:** a single link type already supports traversal in both directions through its two sides; the docs say there is no need to define a separate reverse link type.
- ✗ **C. Single foreign key:** one stored id cannot represent a technician holding many certifications.
- ✓ **D. Join table dataset (correct):** the documented backing for many-to-many links and the requirement for editing them.

## Key idea
Back many-to-many relationships, especially editable ones, with a join table dataset.
Q012730:
## When a link needs its own data
Foreign key and join table links connect two objects but carry no information of their own. The create link type guide describes object-backed link types for this case: an intermediary object type sits between the two sides, backs the link and can hold extra properties.
## How it is built
- Create the object types on both sides (`Flight`, `Crew Member`).
- Create the backing object type (`Crew Assignment`) with properties such as role and assigned date.
- Create many-to-one link types from the backing type to each side, then the object-backed link type.
The docs' own example is a `Flight Manifest` object linking `Aircraft` and `Flight`, with `Pilot` and `First Mate` as properties. Object-backed links also support restricted views.
Example: assignment `CA-7731` links flight `LH-402` and crew member `E-118`, role `Purser`, assigned 2026-11-02.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. One link type per role:** multiplies link types for data that is really an attribute, and still leaves the date without a home.
- ✗ **B. Properties on Crew Member:** one value per person cannot describe many flights; each new flight overwrites the last.
- ✓ **C. Object-backed link (correct):** the intermediary object stores per-relationship properties such as role and assignment date.
- ✗ **D. Extra join table columns:** join tables map the two primary keys; the docs offer object-backed links when the link needs metadata.

## Key idea
When a relationship needs its own properties, back it with an intermediary object type.
Q012731:
## Deletions are not ordinary edits
The how-edits-are-applied page explains conflict resolution between datasource values and user edits, and singles out deletions: once a deletion is applied, the object is no longer visible regardless of the datasource state. If the object is later recreated, it does not inherit the previous edits.
## What this means for builders
- Rebuilding the backing dataset cannot bring a deleted object back.
- To restore it, recreate the object (for example with a create action); expect to re-enter values that users had edited before.
- Delete actions deserve care: restrict them with submission criteria to the people who should remove records.
Example: vehicle `V-2210` is deleted at 10:00; the 11:00 rebuild still contains its row, but the object stays hidden until someone recreates it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Reserved key:** the docs describe recreating an object with the same primary key, so the key is not blocked forever.
- ✓ **B. Deletion wins over the datasource (correct):** the docs say deleted objects stay invisible regardless of the source, and recreation starts without old edits.
- ✗ **C. Failed rebuild:** even a successful build does not undo an action deletion.
- ✗ **D. Recycle bin:** the docs describe no timed restore; there is no mechanism to directly undo a deletion other than recreating the object.

## Key idea
An action deletion hides the object regardless of the backing data; recreate it to bring it back.
Q012732:
## Rules turn parameters into edits
An action type's rules define its effect. Ontology rules create, modify or delete objects and links. The rules page is precise about links:
- **Create link / Delete link** rules work on many-to-many links between objects passed as parameters.
- For **one-to-one and one-to-many (foreign key) links**, you use a Modify object rule and change the foreign key property on the object.
## Why
In a foreign key link the relationship is the property value: a shipment points to the carrier whose primary key equals its carrier code. Changing that value is changing the link.
Example: the `Reassign carrier` action takes the shipment and the new carrier as parameters; a Modify object rule sets the shipment's carrier code to the new carrier's key.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Delete and recreate:** far heavier than needed, and the docs say a recreated object does not inherit the edits made to the deleted one.
- ✗ **B. Schedule rule rebuild:** a rebuild only reflects the source data; the dispatcher's decision must be captured as an edit.
- ✗ **C. Notification rule:** notifications send messages; they do not edit links, and no owner request is needed.
- ✓ **D. Modify object on the foreign key (correct):** the docs say foreign key links are created or removed by editing the foreign key property.

## Key idea
To change a foreign key link in an action, modify the foreign key property; Create link rules are for many-to-many links.
Q012733:
## Object types without data
If every object will be created through actions, you can create the object type without a backing datasource. The create object type guide lists what the helper then asks for:
- **Save in a project**, so the type uses the project-based permission model.
- **An object security policy**, which decides who can view the objects created through actions. Dataset-backed types inherit permissions from the backing data's location instead.
- **A primary key**: every object type still needs one, and each object created through an action must have a unique primary key value.
## Why this fits app-only data
Incidents begin life as user input, so there is no dataset to map. Actions create them, and the Ontology stores them.
Example: the `Report incident` action creates an `Incident` with id `INC-2026-0412`, a location and a severity.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Hand-made empty dataset:** the docs offer a path without any backing dataset for action-only types.
- ✗ **B. No primary key:** every object type requires one, including action-only types.
- ✓ **C. Project, object security policy, unique primary key (correct):** the three requirements the docs list for types without a backing datasource.
- ✗ **D. App sharing decides viewing:** who can view the objects is set by the object security policy, not by the app.

## Key idea
Action-only object types still need a project, an object security policy and a unique primary key per object.
Q012734:
## Submission criteria
Submission criteria (formerly validations) are conditions that decide whether an action can be submitted. They are built from:
- **Current user** conditions: user id, group membership, or other user attributes.
- **Parameter** conditions: values of the action's parameters, including properties of objects passed in.
- Logical operators that combine and nest conditions, plus a failure message shown to the user.
## Why on the action type
The action type is shared by every application. The docs note the failure message appears across Foundry (Object Explorer, Workshop, Quiver) when a condition fails, so one definition protects every place the action is used.
Example: conditions "current user's groups include Maintenance Planners" and "part status is In stock", failure message "Only planners can approve in-stock parts".

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Submission criteria (correct):** they combine user and parameter conditions on the action itself, enforced wherever it runs.
- ✗ **B. Marking on status:** markings control who can see data; seeing a property is not a business rule about approving.
- ✗ **C. Hide the button:** changes one app's interface only; Object Explorer and Quiver would still allow submission.
- ✗ **D. Reverse afterwards:** lets wrong approvals happen first and leaves a window where others act on them.

## Key idea
Put "who may submit and when" in the action type's submission criteria so every app enforces it.
Q012735:
## Avoid NOT on memberships
The submission criteria page warns against NOT conditions on group, marking or organization memberships and calls them a misconfiguration. The platform supports scoped tokens that carry only a subset of a user's permissions. Such a token may not include the attribute the NOT condition checks, so "not in Contractors" passes and grants more access than intended.
## Write the rule positively
State who is allowed rather than who is blocked: for example, "current user's groups include Work Order Closers". A missing attribute then fails the condition, which is the safe direction.
Example: a contractor using a scoped token no longer passes, because the token lacks membership in the allowed group.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Scoped tokens make NOT conditions pass (correct):** the docs advise allow-list conditions on group membership instead.
- ✗ **B. Performance:** the warning in the docs is about security, not speed.
- ✗ **C. Groups not supported:** the Current User template explicitly supports group membership checks.
- ✗ **D. Evaluated daily:** conditions are checked when the action is submitted; the documented problem is the missing attribute, not timing.

## Key idea
Write submission criteria as "must be in an allowed group", never "must not be in a blocked group".
Q012736:
## Two writers to one object
Objects get values from their backing datasource and from user edits made through actions. When both touch the same property, a conflict resolution strategy decides.
## Strategies in the docs
- **Apply user edits (default)**: the edited properties keep the user's value regardless of later datasource updates. Unedited properties still follow the source.
- **Apply most recent value**: a user edit applies only if it is newer than a timestamp property in the datasource. It is set per datasource, needs a Timestamp property in UTC (Date does not work) and is supported on Object Storage v2 object types.
Example: the ticket's `last_updated` timestamp is 09:00 today and the planner's edit was yesterday, so with the second strategy the source priority wins.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Force build:** a force build recomputes datasets but does not change which value wins on an edited property.
- ✗ **B. Failed build:** a successful update still keeps user-edited properties under the default strategy.
- ✗ **C. Edits expire:** edits persist until another edit changes them; the six-hour figure in the docs is how often stored edits are persisted into a Foundry dataset when no new source data arrives, not an expiry.
- ✓ **D. Default user-edits-win, optional most-recent-value (correct):** this is exactly the documented behavior and the alternative.

## Key idea
By default, a property edited by users ignores later source updates unless you switch that datasource to "Apply most recent value".
Q012737:
## Edits are permanent until changed by another edit
The how-edits-are-applied page states that data containing user edits can only be updated by more user edits. There is no mechanism to undo a single edit or deletion other than making another edit, such as running an action again, or recreating the object.
## Tools that exist, and their scope
- **Drop all edits** (Object Storage v2 schema migration) discards every edit on the object type, resetting all objects to the datasource. Useful after testing, far too broad for one mistake.
- Rebuilding the backing data does not remove edits; under the default strategy edited properties keep the user's value.
Example: the planner reruns `Set due date` on work order `WO-5512` with 2026-12-01; the action log keeps both edits.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Rebuild:** edits survive rebuilds; the default strategy keeps user-edited values.
- ✗ **B. Drop all edits:** it discards every edit on the type, not just the latest one per object.
- ✓ **C. Make another edit (correct):** the docs say edited data can only be updated by further user edits, so rerunning the action with the right date is the documented correction.
- ✗ **D. Revert a transaction:** user edits are applied through the Ontology's edit store, not as a transaction you can roll back on the backing dataset.

## Key idea
Fix a wrong user edit with a new edit; dropping all edits resets the whole object type.
Q012738:
## Where user edits live
User edits are applied to the indexed objects at once and stored persistently by the Ontology, not written back into your backing dataset. So the backing dataset shows only what the source sent.
## Materializations
The materializations page describes datasets that contain the latest state of each object by combining input datasources and user edits. Their two main uses:
- Downstream Foundry pipelines that need the latest state including edits.
- Downloads of an object type's current data.
They are optional: user edits work without them, so you create one only for these uses. A materialization can update automatically a few minutes after edits, or periodically to save cost.
Example: the `Order` materialization feeds a weekly fulfilment pipeline that counts orders users cancelled.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Replaying action logs:** rebuilds logic the platform already provides and misses edits made by other paths.
- ✓ **B. Materialized dataset (correct):** the docs name downstream pipelines that need the latest state, including user edits, as a main use of materializations.
- ✗ **C. Exported table:** a manual, partial copy outside lineage, limited to what one app view shows.
- ✗ **D. Force build of the backing data:** user edits never flow back into the source dataset, however it is built.

## Key idea
For pipelines that need user edits, read the object type's materialized dataset, not its backing dataset.
Q012739:
## Names that people see versus names that tools use
Object types and properties carry several names:
- **Display name**: what users see in applications.
- **ID**: a unique identifier used when applications are configured to reference the property.
- **API name**: used in code.
The create object type guide warns that once a property's ID is saved and referenced in user applications, changing it breaks those applications.
## The safe path
Wording for users is a display name change. It improves every app that shows the property without touching the identifiers that the Workshop modules depend on.
Example: display name "Last service date", ID and API name unchanged; all modules keep working and show the new label.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Rename the source column:** unmaps the property from its data and risks the same broken references.
- ✗ **B. Change the ID:** the docs warn this breaks applications that reference the property, and the ID is not the user-facing label.
- ✗ **C. Delete and re-add:** every module loses its reference to the old property, and existing values and edits are tied to the old one.
- ✓ **D. Change the display name (correct):** users see the new wording everywhere, while the saved ID that Workshop modules reference stays intact.

## Key idea
Rename properties for users through the display name; leave saved IDs alone once apps reference them.
Q012740:
## What Machinery is for
The Machinery documentation describes many real-world events as **processes**: entities such as documents, equipment or people change state over time. Machinery lets you understand and manage a process, identify unwanted behaviour and improve it toward a desired outcome.
The docs list purchase-to-pay ("from requisition to payment") as one of the example use cases, next to insurance claims, hospital operations and order-to-cash.
## How it sees the process
- The **process object** is the entity that moves through the process, here an `Invoice`, with a string property that holds its current state.
- **States** (created, approved, paid ...) are nodes; **transitions** between them are edges.
- **Process mining** derives the model automatically from historical observations, and metrics such as time in a state reveal bottlenecks.
## Where the other tools fit
Data integration and pipelines prepare the data Machinery reads; AIP Logic can act on single objects. Neither shows the flow of thousands of invoices through their states.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Machinery (correct):** it is the application the docs name for modelling a process as states and transitions, mining it from historical data and finding bottlenecks, and purchase-to-pay is one of its listed use cases.
- ✗ **B. AIP Logic:** an LLM explaining one invoice at a time does not give a process-wide view of states, transitions and durations.
- ✗ **C. Pipeline Builder:** it can prepare the data, but a list of old invoices says nothing about which step they wait in or which paths they take.
- ✗ **D. Data Connection:** syncing the tables is a prerequisite, not the analysis. Raw tables next to each other do not show the flow.

## Key idea
When the question is "where does this process get stuck", Machinery models the entity's states and transitions and mines the real flow from history.
Q012741:
## What a state is in Machinery
The Machinery core concepts define a **state** as the current condition of an object, for example in progress or delivered for a parcel. Two rules follow:
- The process object type must have a **string property** that holds the state.
- The possible states must be **enumerable**. The docs give the counterexample directly: a `Name` property is not suitable because there are indefinitely many possible names.
Every object must be in exactly one of the possible states at any time, and transitions between states become the edges of the graph.
## Keeping states clean
The docs suggest backing the state property with an **enumeration value type**, so the Ontology data can only take predefined values and Machinery keeps its process states in sync with them.
## Identity is separate
Telling one parcel from another is the job of the object's primary key, not of the state property.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. `name`:** the docs use a name as the example of an unsuitable state, because there are indefinitely many values. Identifying a parcel is the primary key's role.
- ✓ **B. `status` (correct):** it is a string with a small, enumerable set of values describing the parcel's current condition, exactly what the docs require of a state property.
- ✗ **C. `notes`:** free text written in each person's own words is not enumerable, so the graph would get one node per wording instead of a handful of states.
- ✗ **D. `driver_comment`:** changing often does not make a property a state. Comments are free text with unlimited values, which cannot form a fixed set of nodes.

## Key idea
A Machinery state property is a string with an enumerable set of values, such as a status field, never a free-text or identifying field.
Q012742:
## One state at a time
Machinery's core concepts say that every object must be in exactly one of the possible states at any given time. When an entity is naturally in two conditions at once, that is a sign of two processes, not one.
## Process hierarchy
The docs use this very case: an employee can be new-hire or onboarded, and also paid or awaiting payment. These should be **separate processes**, with a **parent process** that tracks whether the employee is payable. In Machinery, process containers can be linked to each other and even nested, and an object type can carry more than one state property (for example a coarse and a granular state), each captured by its own container.
## Why not merge values
Compound states multiply quickly (every onboarding step times every payment step) and hide which part of the work is actually slow.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Drop payroll:** Machinery supports several linked and nested process containers and several state properties on one object type, so nothing needs to be thrown away.
- ✗ **B. List of states:** the docs require one state value per object at a time, held in a string property; a list of simultaneous states is not how Machinery models a process.
- ✓ **C. Separate processes with a parent (correct):** the documentation's answer to an object being in two conditions at once is a process hierarchy, not one overloaded state property.
- ✗ **D. Compound state:** it technically keeps one value, but it multiplies the number of states and mixes two independent flows, which the docs avoid by splitting the processes.

## Key idea
If an entity is in two conditions at once, model two processes under a parent process instead of forcing both into one state.
Q012743:
## Latest state versus history
The Machinery docs connect a process to two kinds of object data:
- **Process objects** such as `Claim` hold the **latest** state. The docs state that the process object type "cannot inform on state transitions and temporal patterns".
- **Log objects** record each individual change: a reference to the process object, the old state, the new state and the timestamp (with optional duration and path).
## Why the log matters
Patterns in paths and metrics such as average time in a state need the time dimension of each change. Machinery can install a standard solution that builds the log object type for you, from platform edit history or from an external changelog dataset. In mining, the docs say a log object type is recommended over mining only the latest state values.
Example: a log row `claim-17, submitted -> under review, 2026-05-03 09:14` is what lets Machinery count that transition and measure the wait.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Enumeration value type:** it keeps state values clean and in sync, but a clean current value is still only the latest state with no history behind it.
- ✗ **B. Workshop widget:** the widget displays metrics, but it reads them from the same process and log objects. Without a log, there is no history for it to show.
- ✗ **C. Nested container:** containers model related or child processes, not storage for transitions. The history of one claim still needs a log.
- ✓ **D. Log object type (correct):** only a record of each change with old state, new state and timestamp lets Machinery derive transitions, paths and durations; the current-state object cannot.

## Key idea
Process objects give the current state; a log object type of timestamped state changes is what reveals paths and time in each state.
Q012744:
## Two sources of state changes
Machinery's log setup can track edits from two places:
- **Platform edits**: if the process object type is edited in Foundry, edit history can be enabled and included in the log.
- **External data**: if changes happen outside the platform, you provide a dataset in **standard changelog format**.
## The changelog format
The docs list its columns: `processId` (the entity), `state` (the new state entered), `timestamp` (when the transition occurred) and an optional `isDeleted` flag. Machinery then installs a product with a Pipeline Builder pipeline that turns these rows into the log object type, and computes derivations such as the previous state, the duration between states and the path taken.
## What not to do
The docs say the log object type is maintained automatically by Machinery, and you should not define actions on it yourself.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Changelog dataset (correct):** for processes outside the platform the docs require a dataset that records which object entered which state at what time, which Machinery turns into its log.
- ✗ **B. Action on the log type:** the docs say the log object type is maintained by Machinery and you should not define actions on it yourself.
- ✗ **C. Overwriting snapshot:** it keeps only the current ward, so any move between two snapshots is lost and timestamps of transitions are unknown.
- ✗ **D. Free-text export with an LLM:** Machinery does not infer states from prose. It expects structured rows with an id, a state and a timestamp.

## Key idea
For external processes, give Machinery a changelog dataset of process id, new state and timestamp; it builds and maintains the log itself.
Q012745:
## Two ways to build a process model
The Machinery docs give two routes:
- **Process mining** derives the model automatically from **historical observations**. Mining is a dedicated mode once a data connection exists, and shows the states and transitions found in the data.
- **Manual drawing** suits a process you have in mind (for example a physical process) or an existing model you want to modify. You start with a process container, add an initial state, the following states, and the actions and automations between them.
## They work together
Mining overlays what the data shows on the current definition, so a hand-drawn model can later be checked against real data. And linking concrete actions and automations to a drawn graph gradually turns the model into an implementation.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Draw first for everyone:** mining can create the model from history on its own; it is not limited to monitoring an already drawn process.
- ✗ **B. Swapped routes:** mining needs data, so it cannot model a process with none. Noise in old data is handled by the mining filters, not by avoiding mining.
- ✓ **C. Mine where history exists, draw where it does not (correct):** years of state changes are what mining needs, and a process with no data can only be drawn from the planned design.
- ✗ **D. Wait for data:** the docs offer manual drawing precisely for processes you have in mind, so a new process does not have to run before it is modelled.

## Key idea
Mine a process model from historical state changes when you have them; draw it by hand when the process is new or you want to adjust a model.
Q012746:
## Mining produces noise
The process mining docs warn that collected data often contains noise and errors, so raw mining output can be too complex or contain unexpected results. Machinery gives two filters:
- **Transition filter**: transitions are ranked by how often they occur, and only the top x % of the cumulative total are kept, cutting off the tail of infrequent transitions.
- **Excluded elements**: a list of erroneous state values or transitions that must not enter the process definition. The list is saved and can be managed over time.
## Why not fix it by deleting data
The source data is still the record of what happened. Filtering the mining result shapes the model without destroying evidence that rare paths exist, which may matter later when looking for deviations.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Accept the full graph:** the docs describe no automatic one-percent cut-off for mining; the builder sets the transition filter and exclusions.
- ✓ **B. Transition filter and excluded elements (correct):** these are the mining filters the docs provide for cutting infrequent transitions and keeping erroneous values out of the definition.
- ✗ **C. Process objects only:** the docs recommend a log object type for mining. Mining only latest values loses transitions instead of filtering the noisy ones.
- ✗ **D. Delete source rows:** it destroys real history to tidy a picture, and the same problem returns with new data. The docs handle it with filters in mining instead.

## Key idea
Tame a noisy mined process with the transition filter and an excluded-elements list, not by deleting source data.
Q012747:
## Reading the mining overlay
In mining mode, Machinery overlays the existing process definition with the states and transitions found in the data. The docs give three styles:
- **Amber**: the mining result, elements that will be added to the definition once you confirm.
- **Gray**: elements that occur in the data and already exist in the definition.
- **Dashed line**: elements of the current definition that have **no reference in the data**, which may indicate an issue with the process definition.
## What to do with it
A dashed transition invites a question: does the real process skip this step (for example refunds are issued before inspection), is the step recorded under a different state value, or is it simply rare? Mining turns a drawn model into something that can be checked against what actually happens.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Already known:** elements found in the data that already exist in the definition are shown in gray, not dashed.
- ✗ **B. Automation:** the mining styles describe whether an element is in the data and the definition, not whether a person or an automation caused it.
- ✗ **C. New finding:** newly mined elements are shown in amber and are added on confirmation; dashed means the opposite, present only in the definition.
- ✓ **D. In the definition but not in the data (correct):** the docs use the dashed style for definition elements with no reference in the data, a hint that the drawn process may not match reality.

## Key idea
In Machinery mining, amber is new from data, gray is confirmed by data, and dashed is drawn but never seen in the data.
Q012748:
## The graph describes, the data decides
Machinery's states are tied to data: the state ID in Machinery equals the string value of the object's state property. The docs are explicit about what editing the graph does not do:
- Changing the name of a state in Machinery **does not change values in your data**.
- Changing the state value in Machinery does **not update dependencies** such as action submission criteria or automations triggered by a state condition.
## Showing a friendlier label
To change the label shown on the graph, the docs say to **overwrite the display name** and keep the state ID equal to the data value. Backing the state property with an enumeration value type keeps Machinery's states in sync with the allowed values.
## Practical rule
Treat the graph as a model of the process. Changing what the process really does means changing the data, the actions and the automations themselves.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Model, not data (correct):** the docs state that renaming a state in Machinery changes neither the Ontology values nor dependencies such as submission criteria; a display name is the way to relabel it.
- ✗ **B. Locked states:** the rename did take effect in the graph. What it does not do is reach the data and the action's criteria.
- ✗ **C. Ontology rejected it:** nothing was sent to the Ontology. The graph edit simply does not touch the data.
- ✗ **D. Wait for a build:** the log pipeline computes log entries from data; it never rewrites the process object's state values or an action's criteria.

## Key idea
Renaming a state in Machinery changes only the model; data values and action criteria stay as they are, so use a display name for labels.
Q012749:
## What causes a state change
The Machinery core concepts are direct: **actions are the cause of state transitions**. State changes that happen within the platform are defined by an action, and you can import those actions into the Machinery graph and describe their role in the process.
## How the graph shows it
- **Input states**: the states an object may be in before the action. For Foundry actions this can be enforced through submission criteria.
- **Output states**: the possible results, for example "extraction succeeded" or "extraction failed".
- **Automations**: an action that is triggered automatically when one of its input states is reached.
Linking concrete actions and automations to the drawn graph gradually turns the process model into a process implementation.
## What the other parts do
The log object type records changes after they happen, mining reads history to build a model, and the widget displays metrics and filters objects. None of them changes an object's state.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Log object type:** it records each change after the fact and is maintained by Machinery; it is a history, not the cause of the change.
- ✗ **B. Machinery widget:** selecting a node filters the widget's output object set by state; it does not edit the objects.
- ✓ **C. Action (correct):** the docs say actions cause state transitions inside the platform, and the graph shows each action between its input states and its output states.
- ✗ **D. Process mining:** it derives a model of states and transitions from historical data; it never moves live objects to another state.

## Key idea
In Machinery, actions (and automations, which are triggered actions) cause state transitions; logs, mining and the widget only record, model or display them.
Q012750:
## From bottleneck to action
The Machinery widget renders the process graph in Workshop with metric views such as current count, historical count, current duration and historical duration. It is built to go from "where is it slow" to "which objects":
- **Duration distribution** shows time spent in states; selecting buckets or a range filters the output object set.
- **Node and edge selection** filters objects by state or transition, and can be combined with the chart selection.
- **Output object sets** update automatically and can feed the rest of the Workshop module, for example a table with an action to reassign or escalate.
## Why this matters
The course framing is that process mining should show where to act. Turning the slowest objects into an object set inside the same app keeps the decision next to the evidence.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Separate container for slow ones:** containers model entities or subprocesses, not a slowness filter. Duration is a metric of the existing process.
- ✓ **B. Duration distribution selection (correct):** the docs describe combining a state selection with duration buckets to find objects that take too long, and the selection drives the widget's output object set.
- ✗ **C. Export an image:** a picture carries no objects, so the team must repeat the search by hand in another system, which loses the link between finding and action.
- ✗ **D. Logic summary:** an LLM description of slow cases is not a filtered set of shipment objects the team can work through, and the widget already filters precisely.

## Key idea
In the Machinery widget, select a state and long-duration buckets to turn a bottleneck into an output object set people can act on.
Q012751:
## Conformance filtering
The Machinery widget documentation says that, by default, it displays only processes that **conform to the process definition**:
- States and transitions that are not present in Machinery are excluded.
- Metrics are computed only over conforming processes.
- If any log object type on the graph contains more than 1M objects, conformance filtering is disabled and all input objects are covered.
**Deviating objects**, those that take any state or transition not in the definition, are hidden by default; the viewer can choose to show them and whether to include them in the output.
## Reading the gap
Here 800 orders deviate from the model. That gap is information: either the definition is missing a real path (mine again and add it) or the orders really went off-process and deserve a look.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Fixed display limit:** the docs describe no such cap; the only size rule mentioned is that conformance filtering turns off when a log has more than 1M objects.
- ✓ **B. Conformance filtering (correct):** the widget hides deviating objects by default and computes metrics over conforming processes, which explains fewer orders than the input set.
- ✗ **C. Indexing lag:** the standard log trails changes by one build and one indexing job, a few minutes; it would not explain a gap that has stayed the same for a week.
- ✗ **D. Parent links:** inputs are configured per root process and subprocess sets are derived from links; root orders do not need a parent to be counted.

## Key idea
The Machinery widget hides objects that deviate from the defined process by default, so a count gap points to off-model paths.
Q012752:
## AIP Logic in one sentence
The documentation calls AIP Logic a **no-code development environment for building, testing and releasing functions powered by LLMs**. A Logic function:
- takes **inputs** such as Ontology objects, object sets or text strings,
- is composed of **blocks** (Use LLM, Apply action, Execute function, loops, conditionals, variables),
- returns an **output**: a value, an object, or edits to the Ontology.
## Why it exists
Builders get AI-powered functions that use the Ontology without managing development environments and API calls themselves. Logic functions are then used like any other function: in Workshop, behind actions, or in automations.
## What it is not
It is not a model training tool; the Use LLM block uses models already available in the platform, following Palantir's multi-model approach.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. No-code LLM function builder (correct):** this is the docs' own definition, with inputs like objects or strings and outputs that can be values or Ontology edits.
- ✗ **B. Fine-tuning service:** Logic writes prompts and uses available models; training a private model is not what it does.
- ✗ **C. Free-form chat:** Logic builds and releases reusable functions; it is not a chat window over datasets.
- ✗ **D. Code template with own keys:** the docs stress that Logic avoids the complexity of development environments and API calls; models come from the platform.

## Key idea
AIP Logic is a no-code way to build, test and release LLM-powered functions that read from and act on the Ontology.
Q012753:
## Proposing edits versus making them
When you run a Logic function inside AIP Logic, the Debugger shows the **proposed** Ontology edits, but the docs say they are **not executed**. Edits reach the Ontology only when the function is called **from an action** (or from an automation).
## The documented path
1. Give the function a way to edit: an Apply actions tool in a Use LLM block, or an Apply action block.
2. **Publish** the Logic function when you are done iterating.
3. **Create an action backed by** the published function.
4. Use that action in a **Workshop** module to power the workflow.
## Where Logic files live
A new Logic file must be saved in a project folder, not in a home folder, and permissions come from the platform's normal security model, not from a special grant to the function.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Run it by hand:** runs inside AIP Logic only propose edits, and copying results manually defeats the purpose of putting the decision in the app.
- ✗ **B. Edit permission on the function:** there is no such grant; the docs require calling the function from an action for edits to be written.
- ✓ **C. Publish, back an action, use it in Workshop (correct):** this is the sequence the docs give for turning a Logic function's proposed edits into real Ontology changes from an app.
- ✗ **D. Home folders:** Logic files must be saved in a project folder, and copies per user would split one function into many unmanaged versions.

## Key idea
A Logic function changes the Ontology only when it is published and called from an action, which a Workshop app can then use.
Q012754:
## The Debugger
After a Logic function runs, the **Debugger** opens and shows the LLM's **chain of thought** for each block. The docs describe it as the place to see each step of the model's "thought process" and information on the **tools** it used. You can expand block cards and review the **generated prompts**.
## A sensible first step
Before rewriting a prompt or swapping a model, look at what actually happened:
- Did the prompt contain the complaint text and the properties you expected?
- Did the model call the search tool, and what did the tool return?
- Did a later block misread an earlier block's output?
Recent runs can be reopened from the Run panel to see their output and debug log.
## Metrics have another job
Function metrics (success and failure counts, execution duration) show health over time; they do not explain why one answer was wrong.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Usage metrics:** counts and durations describe overall health, not the reasoning inside one run, and this run did not fail, it gave a poor answer.
- ✗ **B. Ontology Manager:** it describes the object type, not what a particular Logic run read or decided; run details live in the Debugger.
- ✗ **C. Source data first:** data can be the cause, but guessing skips the evidence. The Debugger shows whether the data even reached the prompt.
- ✓ **D. Debugger (correct):** it shows the chain of thought, prompts and tool calls of the specific run, which is the evidence needed to see why the answer went wrong.

## Key idea
To understand a single bad Logic result, start with the Debugger's chain of thought, prompts and tool calls for that run.
Q012755:
## The model sees only what you give it
The AIP Logic docs say it plainly: when composing a prompt, keep in mind that an LLM **only has access to what you specifically provide**. Having an object as a function input does not put its properties into the prompt.
## Giving the model the data
In the prompt you reference variables available at that point, such as inputs and earlier block outputs, and for an object you choose which of its properties to insert. Here the prompt should include the customer's contract end date (and anything else the reminder needs).
## Recommended prompt shape
The docs suggest starting with the most important information (an overview of the task), then the data the LLM needs, then guidance on when to use tools.
## The usual wrong fixes
A bigger model, a longer prompt or broad tool access all add cost and still leave the key fact out.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Longer generic prompt:** more general guidance does not supply this customer's contract date; the gap is data, not instructions.
- ✓ **B. Properties not referenced (correct):** the docs state that an LLM only sees what the prompt provides, so the contract end date must be inserted from the customer input.
- ✗ **C. Query tools for everything:** the needed object is already an input, and broad tool access is slower and less precise than inserting the property directly.
- ✗ **D. Bigger model:** no model can mention a date it was never shown; switching models adds cost without adding the missing data.

## Key idea
In AIP Logic, the LLM sees only what the prompt references, so insert the needed object properties instead of reaching for a bigger model or longer prompt.
Q012756:
## Tools in a Use LLM block
A Use LLM block is made of a **prompt**, **tools** and an **output**. Tools let the model reach beyond its own text generation; the docs list:
- **Apply actions**: edit the Ontology through actions.
- **Call function**: call code-defined functions or other Logic functions.
- **Query objects**: read chosen object types and properties.
- **Calculator tool**: perform **accurate mathematical calculations** with an LLM.
## Why a tool beats a better prompt
Language models generate text; arithmetic done "in the head" of a model can be wrong in ways that prompting reduces but does not remove. Handing the calculation to a tool makes it exact, and the Debugger shows the tool call so the result can be checked.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Calculator tool (correct):** the docs describe it as the tool for accurate mathematical calculations with an LLM, which removes the arithmetic from the model's guesswork.
- ✗ **B. Fewer line items:** shorter lists change how often errors appear, not why; the business still needs correct totals for long quotes.
- ✗ **C. Newer model:** no model is guaranteed exact at arithmetic, and swapping models adds risk without addressing the cause.
- ✗ **D. Prompt to double-check:** it may reduce errors but still relies on the model computing in text, which is what fails here.

## Key idea
When a Logic function needs exact numbers, give the Use LLM block the Calculator tool instead of trusting the model's arithmetic.
Q012757:
## Reuse instead of re-implementing
The AIP Logic **Execute function** block calls existing functions in Foundry, including TypeScript, Python and other Logic functions. The docs give the reason directly: it lets you **reuse existing functions** that already do the task rather than implementing the logic again.
## Chaining blocks
Blocks pass their outputs to later blocks. Here the risk score from the Execute function block becomes an input to the Use LLM block, whose prompt can reference it.
## Why the deterministic part stays in code
A tested function returns the same score for the same supplier. Asking a language model to re-derive it from rules in the prompt makes a reliable number unreliable, and copying the logic creates a second version that will drift.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Rebuild with variables:** duplicating tested logic inside Logic creates a second copy to maintain, which the Execute function block exists to avoid.
- ✗ **B. Rules in the prompt:** the model may apply them inconsistently, turning a deterministic score into a guess, and the rules now live in two places.
- ✓ **C. Execute function block (correct):** it reuses the tested TypeScript function, and its output can be chained into the Use LLM block, exactly the reuse the docs describe.
- ✗ **D. Nightly spreadsheet:** the score goes stale and leaves the governed function path; the function can be called directly at run time.

## Key idea
Reuse existing platform functions in AIP Logic with the Execute function block rather than re-creating their logic in prompts or blocks.
Q012758:
## Two ways to apply an action in Logic
- **Apply actions tool** (inside a Use LLM block): the model decides whether and how to call the action, guided by the prompt. Useful when judgement is needed.
- **Apply action block**: calls an action **deterministically**, without going through an LLM. The docs say it gives **precise control over how parameters are filled** and **speeds up execution**; their own example sets a priority status on an incident.
## Choosing
If a rule is fixed (critical means high), there is nothing for a model to judge. A deterministic block is faster, cheaper and predictable. Keep LLM blocks for the parts that need reading or reasoning over unstructured input. A conditional block can route different cases down different paths when the rule has branches.
Either way, the edit is written only when the Logic function runs from an action or automation.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Query objects tool:** it lets the model read data but not apply the edit, and it still makes a fixed rule depend on model judgement.
- ✗ **B. Apply actions tool:** it leaves a fixed rule to the model's judgement, so the parameter could differ between runs and each run pays for an LLM call.
- ✗ **C. Call another Logic function:** it adds a second model for a rule that needs no model at all, making the step slower and less predictable.
- ✓ **D. Apply action block (correct):** it calls the action without an LLM, filling parameters exactly as configured, which the docs describe as precise and faster.

## Key idea
When an edit follows a fixed rule, use the deterministic Apply action block; keep LLM tools for steps that need judgement.
Q012759:
## Two different questions
- **Why did this one result go wrong?** The **Debugger** answers it: it shows the chain of thought, the generated prompts and the tool calls of a single run.
- **Is the function healthy over time?** The AIP Logic overview says you can monitor the health and performance of Logic functions through **metrics, including success and failure counts and execution duration**.
## Why the run history is not enough
Recent runs can be reopened with their output and debug log, but in the default **user-scoped** execution mode you can only see your own execution logs. A lead looking at their own runs sees a small, unrepresentative slice.
## Example
If failures rose from 1% to 6% after a model change two weeks ago, the failure count trend shows it at once; the Debugger then helps explain individual failing runs.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Debugger of a new run:** it explains one run's reasoning and tool calls; one fresh run says nothing about failure rates or speed over two weeks.
- ✗ **B. Own runs in the Run panel:** in the default user-scoped mode each user sees only their own execution logs, so this misses everyone else's runs.
- ✗ **C. Machinery graph:** Machinery models how objects move through states; it does not measure the failure rate or duration of a Logic function.
- ✓ **D. Monitoring metrics (correct):** the docs name success and failure counts and execution duration as the way to monitor a Logic function's health and performance over time.

## Key idea
Use a Logic function's metrics (success and failure counts, execution duration) for health over time, and the Debugger for why a single run went wrong.
Q012760:
## Using a Logic function in Workshop
The AIP Logic docs list the ways a published Logic function is used, the same way as any function on objects:
- Back an **action** with it and call the action from Workshop (needed for Ontology edits).
- Back a **Markdown widget**: in this case **the output type of the Logic function must be a string**.
- Call it from other Logic functions or functions on objects.
## Matching the output to the consumer
A function's output type is a contract with whatever calls it. A Markdown widget renders text, so it needs text. A function that returns an object or Ontology edits fits other consumers, such as an action.
Example: the function returns "Customer reported repeated outages since May; two site visits; awaiting part 47-B." and the widget renders it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. No inputs:** the docs set a rule on the output type, not on inputs; functions used in Workshop commonly take objects from the module.
- ✓ **B. String output (correct):** the docs state that a Logic function backing a Markdown widget must return a string, so returning the summary text fixes the mismatch.
- ✗ **C. Project-scoped mode:** execution mode decides whose permissions are used and who sees logs, not whether a widget can call the function.
- ✗ **D. Apply an edit:** edits are for actions; the Markdown widget displays the function's string output directly, not a saved property.

## Key idea
Match a Logic function's output to its consumer: a Workshop Markdown widget needs a string output.
Q012761:
## Execution modes
The AIP Logic docs describe two execution modes:
- **User-scoped** (the default): the function runs with the **permissions of the user running it**, and **you can only see your own execution logs**.
- **Project-scoped**: the function runs with the **permissions of the project containing the function**, and **logs are visible to everyone with project access**.
## It is a real tradeoff
The mode decides two things at once: whose permissions apply when the function reads and writes, and who can see run logs. Before switching, the team should be sure that project-level permissions are appropriate for what the function reads, because every caller then runs with them.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Admins only:** in project-scoped mode every project member can see the logs, so no request process is needed.
- ✗ **B. Service account ownership:** the docs describe no file-owner rule for logs; visibility follows the execution mode.
- ✓ **C. User-scoped versus project-scoped (correct):** the default user-scoped mode limits logs to your own runs; project-scoped mode uses project permissions and makes logs visible to everyone with project access.
- ✗ **D. Wait a week:** the docs tie log visibility to the execution mode, not to how long the function has been published.

## Key idea
In AIP Logic, user-scoped mode shows each user only their own logs; project-scoped mode uses project permissions and shares logs with the project.
Q012762:
## Tools run on the user's behalf
The AIP Logic blocks page is explicit: LLMs **do not have direct access to tools**. They can only **ask** to use tools, and AIP Logic executes those calls **within the invoking user's permissions**. The overview adds that Logic is built on the same security model as the rest of the platform, granting an LLM access only to what is necessary.
## Read-time controls
Row and column controls such as restricted views, object security policies and property security policies filter what the model can read on the user's behalf. The model can never see data the user is not authorized to read.
## One caveat the docs add
These controls apply at read time. They do not extend to the model's output or the edits it composes, so data that must stay protected downstream should also carry a marking.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Tools run as the user (correct):** the model only requests tool calls and AIP Logic executes them with the invoking user's permissions, so a user without salary access cannot expose salaries through the tool.
- ✗ **B. Builder's permissions:** configuring the tool does not lend the builder's access to later callers; each call is checked for the user running it.
- ✗ **C. Service identity:** the docs say tool calls run within the invoking user's permissions; removing data from the Ontology is unnecessary.
- ✗ **D. Prompt instruction:** Logic does not rely on asking the model to ignore data; the platform never gives the model data the user cannot read.

## Key idea
In AIP Logic, the model only requests tool calls, which run with the invoking user's permissions, so it cannot read what the user cannot.
Q012763:
## Read-time enforcement only
The AIP Logic docs carry a specific warning. Row and column access controls (restricted views, object security policies, property security policies) **filter what the model can read** on a user's behalf. They **do not extend to the model's output or to any Ontology edits it composes**.
## Why that matters here
An authorized user's run can read restricted details, and the model can repeat them in a summary. If that summary is written to a widely shared object, the protection of the source rows does not follow it.
## The documented remedy
To keep data protected as it flows downstream, the docs say to pair these controls with a **marking** or **Classification-based Access Control**. Markings propagate through logic, so derived data stays protected.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Logic cannot be used:** the docs describe how such controls filter reads in Logic; they do not forbid Logic on those object types.
- ✗ **B. Prompt instruction:** asking the model to be careful is not an access control, and the docs name markings, not prompts, as the remedy.
- ✗ **C. Controls cover outputs:** the docs say the opposite; read-time controls stop at what the model reads.
- ✓ **D. Pair with a marking (correct):** the docs state read-time controls do not cover the model's output or edits, and recommend markings or classification-based controls to protect data downstream.

## Key idea
Restricted views and object policies protect what a Logic function reads, not what it writes; add a marking to protect outputs downstream.
Q012764:
## Branching for Logic
The AIP Logic docs say to **use Foundry Branching to develop Logic functions in isolation**. On a branch you can publish the function for use in **branch-aware applications such as Workshop**, and merge the changes through an **approved proposal**.
## Seeing what changed
The version history offers a comparison view that shows which blocks were edited, added or removed between two versions, which helps reviewers of the proposal.
## Why not the shortcuts
- Editing the live function exposes users to an untested change, whatever the hour.
- Copies under new names split one function into several, and every consumer must be repointed and later cleaned up.
Branching keeps one function, lets people try the change in context, and puts a review step before it reaches everyone.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Branch, test, merge by proposal (correct):** the docs describe branching to develop Logic in isolation, trying it in branch-aware Workshop, and merging through an approved proposal.
- ✗ **B. Duplicate and repoint:** it creates parallel versions and manual repointing, while branching keeps one function and merges the change safely.
- ✗ **C. Wait for a release:** Logic functions are changed and published by builders; they do not depend on platform upgrades.
- ✗ **D. Quiet-hour edit:** it still changes production without a test or review; a quiet hour only reduces how many people are hit at first.

## Key idea
Change a Logic function that live apps use on a Foundry branch, test it in branch-aware Workshop, and merge through a proposal.
Q012765:
## The Object Table's active object
The Object Table has two output variables, and other widgets (such as an Object View in a details panel) read them:
- Active object: the currently active (highlighted) row, as an object set.
- Selected objects: the checked rows, only populated when multi-select is enabled.
By default the first row is automatically set as the active object when the table loads. A details panel bound to the active object therefore shows a shipment before anyone has chosen one. The table has a setting to disable active object auto-selection, which leaves the active object empty at load time.
## Example
The panel's Object View reads `Object table 1 Active object`. With auto-selection disabled it stays empty until a dispatcher clicks a shipment.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Auto-refresh:** it reloads module data when watched objects change; it does not clear the active object or stop auto-selection.
- ✓ **B. A=Disable auto-selection (correct):** the documented default fills the active object with the first row; turning it off leaves the panel empty until a real choice.
- ✗ **C. Sort the table:** the first row is still auto-selected, so dispatchers still see a shipment they did not choose; sorting only changes which one.
- ✗ **D. Multi-select:** it adds the Selected objects output for checked rows; the active object is still set to the first row at load time.

## Key idea
An Object Table makes its first row the active object at load unless auto-selection is disabled.
Q012766:
## Four building blocks of a module
- Widgets: display content and are the core building blocks of the interface (Object Table, Filter List, Button Group, Metric Card).
- Variables: configure how data moves through a module. A widget has input variables (the data it shows) and output variables (what it produces, such as the selected object or a filter).
- Events: trigger specific behavior when a user acts, for example open an overlay, switch page or set a variable value.
- Layouts: organize the interface into the header, pages, sections and overlays.
## Example
A Filter List writes an object set filter variable, the Object Table reads an object set filtered by it, a Button Group button fires an event that opens a drawer, and the page layout puts the filter on the left and the table on the right.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Storage, arrangement, filters, Actions:** saving values across sessions is state saving, screen arrangement is the layout, filters live in variables, and Actions run from widgets such as buttons.
- ✗ **B. Object types, access, refresh, aggregation:** object types are defined in the Ontology, access comes from roles on the module and data, and aggregations are a variable definition type.
- ✓ **C. B=Display, carry data, trigger, organize (correct):** each job matches the Workshop core concepts pages for widgets, variables, events and layouts.
- ✗ **D. Builds, columns, audit, permissions:** Workshop does not build pipelines, variables are not dataset columns, and module permissions come from roles, not layouts.

## Key idea
Widgets show, variables carry data, events react to users, layouts arrange the screen.
Q012767:
## How a filter reaches a table
A Filter List does not change other widgets by itself. Its output is an object set filter variable: a set of property and value pairs that captures what the user picked.
- The filter output must be applied to the object set variable that backs the table (in the getting-started tutorial, the table's object set is defined as a filter "using a variable" that points to the Filter List output).
- Once applied, every change in the Filter List flows through the variable and the table updates.
- Many filtering widgets work the same way: they output a filter variable that can be applied to object sets or reused in widget configurations.
## Example
`Shipments (filtered)` = Shipment objects filtered by `Filter list 1 Filter output`; the Object Table reads `Shipments (filtered)`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Rebuild per filter:** filtering an object set happens at query time in the app; no pipeline build is involved.
- ✓ **B. C=Filter output not applied (correct):** without wiring the filter variable into the table's object set, the table has no reason to change.
- ✗ **C. Saved state needed:** state saving lets users store and share a view; it is not required for a filter to take effect.
- ✗ **D. Charts only:** the Filter List output can filter any object set variable, and the docs' own tutorial applies it to an Object Table.

## Key idea
A Filter List outputs a filter variable; apply it to the table's object set or nothing changes.
Q012768:
## The filter's input decides its options
The Filter List has an input and an output:
- Input: an object set variable that determines which filter options are available.
- Output: an object set filter variable that is applied to another object set.
If the input is the same set that the output filters, the filter narrows its own options in a loop. The getting-started tutorial therefore says to define a new object set variable to back the Filter List so the filter does not limit the base object set behind it.
## Example
- `All shipments`: Shipment objects, no filter, feeds the Filter List.
- `Shipments (filtered)`: Shipment objects filtered by the Filter List output, feeds the table.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Second table and copying:** adds clutter and manual work while the filter input stays wired to its own output.
- ✗ **B. One object type per status:** status is a property value; splitting the model breaks the shared Ontology to fix an app configuration mistake.
- ✗ **C. Swap to String Selector:** Filter List and Object Table are designed to work together; the problem is the variable wiring, not the widget type.
- ✓ **D. A=Separate unfiltered input (correct):** the filter then always offers every status, and only the table reacts to the user's choice.

## Key idea
Feed a Filter List an unfiltered object set and send its output to the table, never back to itself.
Q012769:
## Two outputs of the Object Table
The Object Table produces two object set outputs:
- Active object: the currently active (highlighted) row. By default the first row becomes active when the table loads.
- Selected objects: the rows a user has checked. It is only populated when multi-select is enabled on the table.
An Action's parameters can default to Workshop variables. A parameter defaulted to the active object only ever receives one shipment; a list parameter defaulted to the selected objects receives every ticked row.
## Example
Turn on multi-select, then set the `Shipments` parameter of Reassign Shipments to `Object table 1 Selected objects`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Loop layout:** a loop shows an embedded module for each object; it does not batch an Action across a selection.
- ✗ **B. One button per row:** Button Groups are not per-row controls, and it would still submit one shipment at a time.
- ✓ **C. B=Multi-select and Selected objects (correct):** this output carries every checked row, so one submission covers the whole selection.
- ✗ **D. Manual Selected property:** selection is user interface state; storing it in the Ontology adds needless writes and model changes.

## Key idea
Active object is one row; Selected objects (with multi-select on) is every ticked row.
Q012770:
## Actions bring their own form
The docs describe Actions as user-friendly, secure building blocks for writeback, defined once as action types and reused in many apps.
- A form is generated automatically from the Action definition, so the writeback and its user interface are not defined separately.
- In Workshop, a Button Group (or the Inline Action widget) exposes the Action. The builder sets parameter defaults from module variables and chooses whether each parameter is visible, hidden or disabled in the form.
- Validation comes from the action type's submission criteria, so the same rules apply in every app.
## Example
The Reassign Shipment action type has parameters Shipment, New Driver and Comment. The button prefills Shipment from the table's active object; the form shows New Driver and Comment for the dispatcher to fill in.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. D=Generated form (correct):** the form follows the action type's parameters, and Workshop only configures defaults and visibility.
- ✗ **B. Separate forms tool:** Workshop shows the Action form inside the module; no other tool or tab is needed.
- ✗ **C. Direct dataset edits:** Workshop writes back through Actions on objects, not by editing the dataset behind them.
- ✗ **D. Input widgets plus a Function:** input widgets exist for other needs, but rebuilding the form duplicates what the Action already provides and loses its validation.

## Key idea
Expose an Action on a button and Workshop shows its generated form; you configure defaults, not fields.
Q012771:
## Parameter defaults in a button
When a Button Group triggers an Action, the builder sets parameter defaults. For each parameter there are two choices:
- Set a default equal to a Workshop variable, such as the Object Table's active object. Then choose how it appears in the form: Visible (prefilled, user may change it), Hidden (not shown at all) or Disabled (shown read-only).
- Leave no default: the field appears empty and the user fills it in.
The getting-started tutorial does exactly this: the alert parameter is set to the table's active object variable and hidden from the form, while the comment is left for the user.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. B=Default from Active object, Hidden (correct):** the Action receives the shipment the dispatcher is viewing and the form only asks for what the dispatcher must decide.
- ✗ **B. Disabled with no default:** Disabled shows a read-only value; with no default the field is simply empty and cannot be filled in.
- ✗ **C. Remove the parameter:** Actions do not infer objects from clicks; the parameter is how the Action knows which object to edit.
- ✗ **D. No default plus a reminder:** keeps the slow, error-prone search that the dispatcher complained about.

## Key idea
Prefill object parameters from module variables and hide or disable them so users only enter real decisions.
Q012772:
## Submission criteria validate the form
An action type can carry submission criteria: conditions on parameters (such as a code matching a pattern) or on the user (a user or group). In the Workshop form:
- Each failing condition shows up as an issue in the form.
- Submission becomes available only when all parameters pass validation.
- After a successful submit, a confirmation toast appears and the object is updated.
Because the rule lives in the action type, every app that uses the Action applies the same check.
## Example
A Destination parameter must match `^[A-Z]{3}$`; typing `Ewr1` flags one issue until the user types `EWR`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Stale object type:** a delayed build may leave data old, but it does not flag an issue on a value the user just typed.
- ✗ **B. Editor role on the module:** Viewer is enough to open and use a module; Editor is for changing the module, not for submitting Actions.
- ✗ **C. Unpublished module changes:** publishing affects which version users see, not whether a valid form can be submitted.
- ✓ **D. C=Failing submission criteria (correct):** the flagged issue on one field and the fact that others submit normally both point to a validation rule on the typed value.

## Key idea
An issue flagged in an Action form means a submission criterion failed; fix the input, not the app.
Q012773:
## Opening versus editing a module
Workshop permissions come from roles on the module itself (directly, through a group, or by default), plus the Organization and Marking requirements:
- By default, users need the Viewer role to open a module and the Editor role to edit it.
- A new module inherits the permissions of the project or folder it is created in.
- Access to the data, Actions and Functions used in the module is permissioned separately from the module.
The Check access panel shows whether a user meets the module's requirement and the extra requirements for its object types, link types, action types and functions.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Never published:** anyone with Editor can edit and save a module; publishing decides what view-mode users get.
- ✓ **B. A=Viewer, not Editor (correct):** the planner can open and use the module, which Viewer allows, but changing its layout needs Editor.
- ✗ **C. Owner on every object type:** editing the module is governed by the module's own roles; data permissions decide what the planner can see and change in the data.
- ✗ **D. Action-type configuration group:** that membership governs creating and editing action types, not editing a Workshop module.

## Key idea
Viewer opens a Workshop module, Editor changes it; data access is a separate question.
Q012774:
## Where a module lives decides who can open it
A Workshop module is a resource like any other file in Foundry:
- It inherits the permissions of the project or folder in which it is created.
- Users need a role on it (Viewer by default to open, Editor to edit), plus the Organization and Marking requirements.
- The data, Actions and Functions it uses are permissioned separately, so the dispatch project should also give dispatchers access to the objects they need.
Keeping the app in the team's project means access follows the project roles that already exist instead of being granted one person at a time.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Publish again:** publishing selects the version users see; it does not open the module to everyone.
- ✗ **B. Names in the header:** the header shows titles, tabs and buttons; it does not control access.
- ✓ **C. D=Save in the team project (correct):** the dispatchers' existing Viewer role there then covers the module.
- ✗ **D. Editor on the sandbox:** grants more than needed (editing) and ties a team app to one person's sandbox.

## Key idea
A module inherits its folder's permissions, so build team apps in the team's project.
Q012775:
## Read-time enforcement in Workshop
The Workshop permissions page says row and column access controls (restricted views, object security policies, property security policies) filter what a user can see in a module:
- Widgets can never display data the user is not authorized to read.
- The same module therefore shows different rows to users with different access.
- These controls apply at read time; they do not extend to widget exports, Action writes or downstream functions, so the docs pair them with markings when data must stay protected downstream.
## Example
A policy lets EMEA dispatchers read only EMEA shipments; one module serves every region without a filter per region.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. B=Row-level controls at read time (correct):** different users seeing different rows in one module is the expected effect of object-level security.
- ✗ **B. Drifting browser caches:** objects are read from the shared Ontology, so two users do not see different data because of cached copies.
- ✗ **C. Auto-refresh off:** auto-refresh reloads when data changes; turning it off cannot remove rows that the other user can see.
- ✗ **D. Interface variables restrict data:** module interface variables pass values into a module; they are not a security control.

## Key idea
Different users can see different rows in one module because Ontology security filters every widget at read time.
Q012776:
## Overlays for temporary steps
Workshop layouts include overlays: drawers that slide in from a side and modals in the center, shown as a layer on top of the selected page.
- A Layers event (Open or Close for each overlay) shows or hides an overlay, typically from a Button Group.
- The design best practices say to use overlays for temporary and secondary interactions, such as completing questionnaires, and to avoid them for analytical sections where users need several layers of information at once.
- They also advise surfacing an element only when the user needs to act on it, to avoid crowding the main view.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Second page:** switching pages takes dispatchers away from their list, which they wanted to keep in view.
- ✗ **B. Always on the main page:** adds a component most users do not need most of the time, against the advice to limit visible components.
- ✓ **C. C=Drawer opened by an event (correct):** the checklist appears only when needed and closes back to the same list and selection.
- ✗ **D. Separate module in a new tab:** splits one task across tabs and loses the selected shipment's context.

## Key idea
Use an overlay for an occasional, secondary step so users keep their place on the page.
Q012777:
## Pages and the header
- Pages let a builder create multi-screen applications. Each page is a blank canvas for its own set of widgets.
- Only the module header persists between pages, so it is the place for module-wide titles, tabs and buttons.
- Layout events (Switch to page) move users between pages; the Tabs widget uses these events, so tabs in the header act as always-visible navigation.
- Within a page, sections can use layouts such as Columns, Rows, Tabs, Flow, Toolbar and Loop.
## Example
Header: title "Dispatch" and tabs Inbox, Depots, Report. Each tab switches to its page.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Separate unlinked modules:** users lose the shared navigation the requirement asks for.
- ✓ **B. D=Pages plus header tabs (correct):** each workflow gets its own canvas and the navigation stays visible because the header persists.
- ✗ **C. One long Flow section:** Flow is a scrolling container for one view; three workflows in one scroll hide navigation and crowd the screen.
- ✗ **D. Collapsible sections on one page:** works for related panels, but three full workflows on one page break the advice to limit components per view.

## Key idea
Separate workflows go on separate pages; put the navigation in the header because only the header persists.
Q012778:
## Loop layouts repeat a module per object
Workshop section layouts include Columns, Rows, Tabs, Flow, Toolbar and Loop.
- A Loop layout loops over an object set or an array and displays an embedded module for each object or entry.
- The card itself is built once as a small module whose interface takes one truck; the loop supplies each truck.
- Because the loop follows the object set, the number of cards changes with the data.
By contrast, Flow is a vertically scrolling container for widgets that run beyond the screen; it does not generate content per object.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Forty copies:** fixed copies break when the count passes 40 and multiply the work for every change.
- ✗ **B. Flow generates cards:** Flow only scrolls its content; repeating per object is the Loop layout's job.
- ✗ **C. Tab per truck, by hand:** manual daily edits to the layout are fragile and show one truck at a time.
- ✓ **D. B=Loop layout (correct):** one card definition, repeated for however many trucks the object set holds.

## Key idea
Repeat the same card for every object in a set with a Loop layout over an embedded module.
Q012779:
